decisions.quote:
This study is a conceptual replication of the study by Han et al. (2015) in which the authors evaluated factors affecting
students’ compliance with emergency instructions during campus emergencies.
decisions.location: Abstract, p. 1, lines 20-21 (full reference on p. 15, lines 839-840)
decisions.reason: The replication paper re-tests a single original study: Han, W., Ada, S., Sharman, R., & Rao, H. R. (2015), 'Campus emergency notification systems: An examination of factors affecting compliance with alerts', MIS Quarterly 39(4), 909-929 (no DOI printed in text). Although the shipped row's outcome_quote comes from this replication paper's abstract, the shipped title_o and doi_o refer to an unrelated ERP study not cited anywhere in the paper. The blind coding (target_index 0) correctly identifies the tested original.

decisions.quote:
Results obtained from the current study indicate mixed support for results from the original study. Results
from the unabridged dataset were consistent with the original study, while those from the verify-first dataset
differed.
decisions.location: Section 5 (Limitations and Future Research), p. 13, lines 735-737
decisions.reason: Evaluated for the resolved target Han et al. (2015). The authors state an explicit overall verdict of mixed support for the original study: the aggregate unabridged dataset supported both H1 (subjective norm) and H4 (information quality trust) in agreement with the original study, whereas the verify-first dataset supported only H4 and category-level results diverged. Both shipped and blind codings agree on 'mixed'.

decisions.quote:
This study is a conceptual replication of the study by Han et al. (2015) in which the authors evaluated factors affecting
students’ compliance with emergency instructions during campus emergencies. The current study focused on broader
public health-related emergencies using eight scenarios evaluated by Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) participants.
decisions.reason: Evaluated for the resolved target Han et al. (2015). The authors collected new survey data from 272 Amazon Mechanical Turk participants across eight public health emergency scenarios to re-test the hypotheses of Han et al. (2015). Both shipped and blind codings agree on 'replication'.
